regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 54.6","signal_text":"India GDP at 7.8% YoY is the headline; the quality test is harder to pass. IIP overall slowed to 6.7% YoY from 8.8%, core sector decelerated to 5.4% YoY from 6%, and PMI manufacturing dipped to 52.8 from 53.5 — three of four activity proxies are losing momentum even as the composite PMI edges up to 54.6. The inversion: capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity is genuinely encouraging, but the last time IIP and core sector diverged this sharply from the GDP headline, the subsequent quarter's GVA print was 150-200bps below the GDP number. Watch GVA, not GDP.","badge_label":"Slowing Pace","badge_type":"b-slow"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 4.45% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"The headline CPI at 4.45% YoY flatters. Decompose it: fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY is at the 95th percentile, WPI at 9.92% YoY is accelerating, and the RBI has already revised its own forecast to 5.1% YoY — above the 5.5% upper tolerance band. The saving grace is core CPI at 3.9% YoY, the lowest in a decade, which tells you demand-side pricing power is absent. The second-order problem: fuel feeds into transport, logistics, and food distribution costs with a 2-quarter lag. Core CPI at 3.9% today is not a guarantee of core CPI at 3.9% in March.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 17.1% YoY; CD ratio 81.4%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 17.1% YoY against deposit growth of 10.8% YoY — a 630bps divergence — with the CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits (75th percentile historically) is the structural fault line. Corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr/month is at the 0th percentile — the lowest on record — meaning wholesale funding markets have effectively closed as an alternative. The historical precedent is instructive: the last time the CD ratio sustained above 80% for more than two quarters, the RBI responded with macro-prudential tightening on risk weights. NBFC credit growth accelerating to 14.9% YoY from 10.6% while their wholesale funding window narrows is the specific stress point to watch.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is on hold, but the RBI's own inflation forecast revision to 5.1% YoY — from 4.6% prior — makes the next move asymmetric: a cut requires fuel inflation to reverse, which Brent at $98.93/bbl does not support. The real rate (repo minus headline CPI) is approximately 80bps — positive but thin. For housing, the average home loan rate at 8.2% p.a. means EMI affordability is already stretched; any upward rate surprise would hit the ₹80 lakh–₹1.5 cr premium segment hardest, precisely where 27% of new launches are concentrated.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.1% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.1% YoY and capacity utilisation rising to 77.4% of capacity from 75.6% — two consecutive months of acceleration — is the most credible signal that private capex is not just budgeted but being executed. The inversion: core sector at 5.4% YoY, which leads actual infrastructure output, decelerated from 6%. Cement and steel dispatch embedded in core sector data typically confirm or deny IIP capital goods within one quarter. If core sector stays below 6% for a third month, the capex narrative gets a significant asterisk.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹199853 cr/mo; PV 16% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹1,99,853 cr/month is a strong number, but the composition matters: two-wheeler sales at 19.7% YoY and passenger vehicle sales at 16% YoY signal that mass-market and aspirational consumption are both running hot — this is not an urban-affluent-only story. The proxy check: e-commerce GMV growth at 18% YoY (26th percentile) is surprisingly subdued relative to vehicle sales, suggesting physical retail and durables are outpacing digital discretionary. Credit card growth at 2.3% YoY — down from 5.6% — is the one soft signal: urban consumers may be spending on big-ticket items financed by vehicle loans (18.8% YoY) rather than revolving credit.","badge_label":"Demand Surge","badge_type":"b-exp"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 17.1% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 10.8% YoY creates a 630 bps divergence. CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits (down from 82.5% prior month) remains elevated at 75th percentile historically. Credit-to-deposit gap has widened for 3 consecutive months: deposits lagging credit acceleration signals funding stress. NBFC credit growth at 14.9% YoY (up from 10.6% prior) and corporate bond issuance at 18,700 ₹ cr / month (at 0th percentile — lowest on record) indicate wholesale funding markets are tightening.","implication":"RBI will face pressure to either cut rates to incentivise deposits or tighten liquidity. Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% — they'll poach deposits from weaker competitors. Avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities; their cost of funds will spike. Expect deposit-linked lending rates to compress margins for smaller lenders. Position for a 25 bps rate cut within 2 quarters if deposit growth doesn't accelerate.","pct_10y":75,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 75th percentile is historically elevated but not yet critical. Prior episodes at this level preceded either RBI rate cuts or NBFC stress — watch for which path emerges.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Cycle Firing on All Cylinders","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.1% YoY (latest) signals robust investment demand. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6% prior month, 74th percentile) — two consecutive months of acceleration. Core sector growth at 5.4% YoY (down from 6% prior) is the only soft spot, but this lags capex by 1-2 quarters. PMI composite at 54.6 index (83rd percentile, up from 54.3 prior) confirms broad-based manufacturing momentum. Order books are filling: vehicle sales at 16.88% YoY, two-wheeler sales at 19.7% YoY.","implication":"Capex cycle is self-reinforcing — rising capacity utilisation will trigger fresh investment orders. Overweight capital goods, cement, and steel stocks. Favour companies with order backlogs > 2 years of revenue. Infrastructure plays (roads, ports, power) will see sustained demand. Expect IIP capital goods to sustain 12-15% growth for next 2-3 quarters. Avoid cyclical stocks with excess capacity — consolidation will accelerate.","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is mid-cycle historically; prior peaks at 80%+ preceded 18-24 month capex booms. Current trajectory suggests we're in the early-to-mid phase of the cycle.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"Retail Equity Inflows Hit Record Highs","data_text":"SIP inflows at 32,297 ₹ cr / month (up from 31,961 ₹ cr / month, 92nd percentile) — rising 2 consecutive months. SIP AUM at 18.62 ₹ lakh cr (up from 18.21 ₹ lakh cr, 93rd percentile) — also rising 2 consecutive months. SIP accounts at 100.18 mn (up from 99.06 mn, 82nd percentile). Domestic institutional investor (DII) equity net flows at 58,502 ₹ cr net / month (100th percentile — all-time high, up from 35,099 ₹ cr prior month). MF AUM at 87.08 ₹ lakh cr (86th percentile, rising 2 consecutive months). Equity MF net inflows at 29,329 ₹ cr net / month (up from 24,697 ₹ cr prior).","implication":"Retail equity participation is at generational highs. Monitor SIP account growth; if it falls below 5% YoY, retail enthusiasm is waning. Hedge with long-dated puts on Nifty 50.","pct_10y":92,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 92nd percentile are near all-time highs. Prior peaks preceded 15-20% corrections within 6-12 months as retail capitulated into weakness.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI Credibility","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (up from 20.05% prior month, 95th percentile — near all-time high). WPI at 9.92% YoY (up from 9.78% prior, 67th percentile). Brent crude at 98.93 $/bbl (69th percentile, flat month-on-month but up from 97.44 $/bbl 5 months ago). Natural gas at 3.115 $/MMBtu (19th percentile, but up from 2.83 $/MMBtu 5 months ago). RBI inflation forecast revised up to 5.1% YoY (from 4.6% prior), now above the 5.5% upper tolerance band. CPI headline at 4.45% YoY (up from 4.38% prior, 41st percentile) — core CPI at 3.9% YoY (28th percentile, lowest in 10 years).","implication":"Fuel inflation is the tail risk to RBI's rate-cut narrative. If Brent sustains above 100 $/bbl or geopolitical shocks spike it to 120 $/bbl, RBI will be forced to hold or hike despite slowing growth. This would be stagflationary. Reduce exposure to rate-sensitive sectors (autos, housing, NBFCs). Overweight energy stocks and commodity exporters. Hedge INR weakness — a weaker rupee will amplify import inflation. Monitor RBI's next inflation forecast; if it revises above 5.5%, rate cuts are off the table.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a 10-year extreme. Prior episodes at this level coincided with RBI rate hikes and equity corrections of 12-18%.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"US Yields Spike, Carry Trades Unwind","data_text":"US 10-year Treasury yield at 5.18% yield (up from 5.11% prior, 94th percentile — near 10-year high). Fed funds rate at 3.63% p.a. (flat, 67th percentile mid). Fed balance sheet at 6,747.704 $ bn (up from 6,730.912 $ bn, 47th percentile mid) — rising 4 consecutive months. US CPI at 3.353% YoY (up from 3.3039% prior, 53rd percentile), US core CPI at 2.4462% YoY (down from 2.4665% prior, 47th percentile). US GDP SAAR at 1.5% SAAR (down from 2.1% prior, 49th percentile). BOJ rate at 1% p.a. (up from 0.75% prior, 86th percentile — highest in 10 years). ECB deposit rate at 2.25% p.a. (up from 2% prior, 59th percentile). DXY at 101.035 index (flat, 53rd percentile mid, but up from 100.2 five months ago).","implication":"US yields are rising into slowing growth — a classic bear-steepener. Carry trades funded in JPY are unwinding as BOJ tightens (now at 1% p.a., highest in a decade). This will pressure EM currencies and equities. INR at 96.15 ₹ (91st percentile, strong depreciation) is a symptom. Reduce leverage in EM portfolios. Overweight USD-denominated assets and short EM FX. India's FII flows will remain volatile — expect outflows if US yields stay above 5.2%. Hedge with long-dated USD calls on INR.","pct_10y":94,"pct_note":"US 10-year yields at 94th percentile are near decade highs. Prior episodes at this level preceded 15-25% EM equity corrections and 8-12% INR depreciation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakness Accelerates Despite RBI Intervention","data_text":"INR at 96.15 ₹ (up from 95.8 ₹ prior, 91st percentile — near 10-year weak). INR has depreciated 3 of last 5 months, trending weaker. FII equity net flows at 29,631 ₹ cr net / month (up from 20,200 ₹ cr prior, 83rd percentile, but volatile — was -3,111.9 ₹ cr net two months ago). DXY at 101.035 index (up from 100.97 prior, 53rd percentile mid, but rising 4 of last 5 months). US 10-year Treasury yield at 5.18% yield (94th percentile) is pulling capital away from India. India's household debt at 42.6% of GDP (51st percentile mid) and corporate debt at 51.9% of GDP (42nd percentile mid) — both moderate but rising.","implication":"RBI is defending INR but losing the battle. This will raise import costs and inflation. Reduce INR exposure; overweight USD-linked assets. Companies with high import content (autos, pharma, electronics) will see margin pressure. Favour exporters (IT, textiles, pharma APIs). Hedge with long-dated USD calls on INR at 97 ₹ strike.","pct_10y":91,"pct_note":"INR at 91st percentile weakness is a 10-year extreme. Prior episodes at this level preceded 12-18 month periods of sustained depreciation and import inflation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Shift","data_text":"Office absorption at 11.6 mn sq ft / quarter (up from 10.5 mn sq ft prior, but 4th percentile — lowest in 10 years). Office vacancy at 14.5% vacant (down from 15.1% prior, 42nd percentile mid). Yet commercial real estate rents in Bengaluru at 163 ₹/sqft/mo (95th percentile, up from 148 ₹/sqft/mo prior) and Mumbai at 335 ₹/sqft/mo (100th percentile, up from 322 ₹/sqft/mo prior) are at all-time highs. Retail mall vacancy at 5% vacant (down from 7.5% prior, 8th percentile — near all-time low). Nifty IT index is flat YTD despite office absorption collapsing. This disconnect reveals the truth: Global Capability Centers (GCCs) — not traditional IT services — are the marginal buyer of office space. GCCs are capital-light, hire locally, and don't need the sprawling campuses that IT services built. Traditional IT services are consolidating and shrinking footprints.","implication":"IT services stocks are value traps. Their real estate is stranded — high fixed costs, declining utilization. GCCs will absorb only premium, centrally-located space (hence Bengaluru and Mumbai rents at all-time highs). Avoid IT services with > 40% of real estate in secondary cities or aging campuses. Overweight GCC-exposed companies (consulting, niche tech services, staffing). Commercial real estate plays should focus on Grade-A, centrally-located assets in Tier-1 cities — these will command 15-20% rental growth. Expect IT services to announce real estate write-downs and consolidation within 2 quarters. This is a 3-5 year structural headwind for the sector.","pct_10y":4,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 4th percentile is a 10-year low, yet rents are at all-time highs — a rare inversion that signals a structural shift in demand patterns, not cyclical weakness.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP, Three Decelerating Proxies — Quality Gap Widens

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY (64th percentile) — but IIP slowed to 6.7% YoY from 8.8% and core sector decelerated to 5.4% YoY from 6.0%.
  • PMI composite at 54.6 (83rd percentile) is rising, but manufacturing sub-index fell to 52.8 from 53.5 — services are carrying the composite.
  • Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile, rising two consecutive months) is the one unambiguous positive — investment demand is real.
  • But GST at ₹1,99,853 cr/month (71st percentile) and two-wheeler sales at 19.7% YoY confirm consumption is broad-based, not just formal-sector noise.

The tension: GDP headline and PMI composite point up; IIP, core sector, and manufacturing PMI point down. The divergence between the services-driven composite and goods-economy deceleration is the gap the next GVA print will close — downward.

Bottom line: Watch core sector YoY: a third consecutive month below 6.0% invalidates the capex-led growth narrative and forces a GDP-GVA reconciliation the market is not pricing.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Surveys Accelerate, US Output Decelerates — Bond Market Knows

The facts:

  • US PMI composite at 56 (84th percentile) signals re-acceleration; but US GDP SAAR slowed to 1.5% SAAR from 2.1% — surveys and output are moving in opposite directions.
  • US 10Y Treasury at 5.18% yield (94th percentile, up from 5.11% prior) is doing the Fed's tightening for it — real economy stress is already embedded in the curve.
  • BOJ rate at 1.0% p.a. (86th percentile, up from 0.75%) is the underappreciated tail: yen carry unwind accelerates as the rate differential compresses.
  • But China PMI composite at 49.5 (contraction) and GDP at 4.3% YoY from 5.0% removes the commodity reflation backstop that EM bulls are counting on.

The tension: DM equity markets are pricing growth re-acceleration; DM bond markets and actual GDP prints are pricing deceleration. China's inability to reflate means the commodity channel that typically rescues EM in a DM slowdown is absent.

Bottom line: BOJ's next move is the single largest tail risk for India liquidity flows — a further 25bps hike would accelerate yen carry unwind and pressure FII positioning in Indian equities.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

Domestic Flows at Record Highs, Wholesale Funding at Record Lows

The facts:

  • DII equity net flows at ₹58,502 cr net/month (100th percentile, all-time high) — SIP inflows at ₹32,297 cr/month (92nd percentile) rising two consecutive months underpin this.
  • FII equity net at ₹29,631 cr net/month (83rd percentile) — but the sequence was -₹3,112 cr two months ago; FII flows are volatile, not structural.
  • But corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr/month is at the 0th percentile — the lowest on record — wholesale funding markets are effectively shut.
  • CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits (75th percentile) with deposit growth at 10.8% YoY vs credit at 17.1% YoY means bank funding stress is not easing.

The tension: Retail equity liquidity has never been stronger; institutional credit liquidity has never been tighter. The two are not offsetting — equity SIPs do not fund NBFC balance sheets.

Bottom line: Watch NBFC commercial paper spreads: if they widen 50bps above the 3-month T-bill, the credit-deposit stress has migrated from a ratio problem to a funding crisis.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

REITs Pricing Absorption Collapse; NRI Demand Reprices Premium Supply

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases at 20% (up from 15%, +5pp), with 25% share within premium/luxury; remittances at $135.46 bn (14% YoY) are the funding source.
  • Supply is chasing NRI demand: luxury (₹1.5–2.5 cr) and ultra-luxury (>₹2.5 cr) together represent 47% of new launches, while affordable (6% — the market has structurally repositioned upmarket.
  • Office REITs are pricing the wrong reality: Embassy at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, Brookfield at ₹263/unit — all down sharply — while Mumbai rents hit ₹335/sqft/mo (100th percentile) and Bengaluru rents ₹163/sqft/mo (95th percentile).
  • But office absorption at 11.6 mn sq ft/quarter (4th percentile) exposes the paradox: GCCs (42% of occupier mix) take smaller, premium footprints — high rent, low volume.

The tension: REIT unit prices are falling while the rents their assets command are at all-time highs. The market is discounting absorption volume; it should be discounting rent per sq ft. The GCC structural shift makes volume a misleading metric.

Bottom line: Office REITs are a contrarian buy if GCC leasing sustains above 40% of absorption mix — watch Q3 occupier-split data from Bengaluru and Hyderabad as the confirmation trigger.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Risks, One Trigger — Fuel, Funding, Flows, and the Fed

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) with Brent at $98.93/bbl — a $5 move to $104 widens CAD by ~40bps, pressures INR past 97, and forces RBI to abandon its pause.
  • CD ratio at 81.4% credit ÷ deposits with corporate bond issuance at a record-low ₹18,700 cr/month — NBFC refinancing risk is the highest since IL&FS; one large NBFC rollover failure cascades.
  • US 10Y at 5.18% yield (94th percentile) — FII equity flows reversed to -₹3,112 cr net/month just two months ago; a further 20bps yield rise likely flips FII flows negative again.
  • BOJ at 1.0% p.a. (86th percentile) — each 25bps hike compresses the yen carry differential and forces EM position liquidation; India's ₹29,631 cr net/month FII inflow is the most exposed.

The tension: All four risks share a common amplifier: INR at 96.15 (91st percentile) has no buffer. A fuel shock, a funding stress event, or a carry unwind — any one of them alone is manageable; two simultaneously is not.

Bottom line: Watch Brent crude this week: a close above $102/bbl triggers the CAD-INR-inflation feedback loop and makes the RBI's pause untenable before the December policy meeting.

"}
